The recursive formulation to compute the table entries is as follows:

[latex] \begin{array}{ll} T[0][k]=T[k][0]=1 & \text { for } k=0,1,2, \ldots, n \\ T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1] & \text { for } 1 \leq i, j \leq n \end{array} [/latex]

Algorithm [latex]B_{k}, k \in\{1,2\}[/latex] is said to be correct if and only if it calculates the correct values of [latex]T[i][j][/latex], for all [latex]0 \leq i, j \leq n[/latex], (as per the recursive formulation) at the end of the execution of the algorithm [latex]B_{k}[/latex].

Consider an array [latex]A[/latex] of integers of size [latex]n[/latex]. The indices of [latex]A[/latex] run from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]n[/latex]. An algorithm is to be designed to check whether [latex]A[/latex] satisfies the condition given below.

[latex]\forall i, j \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}[/latex] such that [latex]i>j,(A[i+1]-A[i])>(A[j+1]-A[j])[/latex]

Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm that can be designed for the problem?
solution:
The condition says: for every pair of indices [latex]i>j[/latex] (both in [latex]\{1,\ldots,n-1\}[/latex]), the consecutive difference [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] must exceed [latex]D[j]=A[j+1]-A[j][/latex]. In other words, the sequence of consecutive differences [latex]D[1],D[2],\ldots,D[n-1][/latex] must be strictly increasing (array [latex]A[/latex] is "convex").

This can be checked with a single linear pass: compute each [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] and verify [latex]D[i]>D[i-1][/latex] for each consecutive pair, stopping early with "no" the first time this fails. This takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] time, and it's optimal since every element of the array must be examined at least once to certify the condition holds.

Answer: [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]

text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be a weighted directed acyclic graph with [latex]m[/latex] edges and [latex]n[/latex] vertices. Given [latex]G[/latex] and a source vertex [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], which one of the following options gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm to find the lengths of shortest paths from [latex]s[/latex] to all vertices that are reachable from [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]{G}?[/latex]
solution:
For a directed acyclic graph (DAG), the fastest known algorithm for single-source shortest paths uses the following two steps: (1) compute a topological ordering of the vertices in [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time, then (2) process vertices in that topological order, relaxing every outgoing edge of each vertex exactly once, which takes [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time in total (this correctly computes shortest paths since, in topological order, all edges into a vertex are relaxed before that vertex is finalized, and no negative cycles can exist in a DAG so ordinary Dijkstra-style priority queues or Bellman-Ford repeated relaxation are unnecessary).

This is strictly faster than Dijkstra's [latex]\Theta(m+n\log n)[/latex] (needed only for general graphs with a priority queue) or the [latex]\Theta(nm)[/latex] Bellman-Ford bound (needed for general graphs, possibly with negative edges but no negative cycles) — the DAG structure lets us avoid both.

Answer: [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex]

Consider a complete graph [latex]K_{n}[/latex] with [latex]n[/latex] vertices ( [latex]n>4[/latex] ). Note that multiple spanning trees can be constructed over [latex]K_{n}[/latex]. Each of these spanning trees is represented as a set of edges. The Jaccard coefficient between any two sets is defined as the ratio of the size of the intersection of the two sets to the size of the union of the two sets.

Which one of the following options gives the lowest possible value for the Jaccard coefficient between any two spanning trees of [latex]K_{n}[/latex] ?
solution:
The Jaccard coefficient between two spanning-tree edge sets is [latex]\dfrac{|E_1\cap E_2|}{|E_1\cup E_2|}[/latex], which reaches its lowest possible value [latex]0[/latex] precisely when the two spanning trees share no edges at all (completely edge-disjoint spanning trees).

In [latex]K_n[/latex] for [latex]n>4[/latex], there are more than enough edges ([latex]\binom{n}{2}[/latex] total, versus only [latex]n-1[/latex] needed per spanning tree) to always construct two entirely edge-disjoint spanning trees (this is guaranteed by well-known results on edge-disjoint spanning trees in dense graphs, e.g. via Nash-Williams/Tutte-style constructions). When the intersection is empty, the Jaccard coefficient is exactly [latex]0[/latex], which is also the theoretical minimum possible value for any Jaccard coefficient.

Answer: 0

text:
Consider an array [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]. Suppose the merge sort algorithm is executed on array [latex]A[/latex] to sort it in increasing order. The merge sort algorithm will carry out a total of [latex]7[/latex] merge operations.

A merge operation on sorted left array [latex]L[/latex] and sorted right array [latex]R[/latex] is said to be void if the output of the merge operation is the elements of array [latex]L[/latex] followed by the elements of array [latex]R[/latex].

The number of void merge operations among these [latex]7[/latex] merge operations is ________. (answer in integer)
solution:
A merge is void when every element of the left sub-array is already [latex]\le[/latex] every element of the right sub-array, so the merge simply concatenates them with no interleaving.

Trace merge sort on [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]:

Bottom level (pairs):
[latex][10],[7]\to[7,10][/latex] (result is [latex]R[/latex] then [latex]L[/latex], not "[latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]") — not void.
[latex][8],[19]\to[8,19][/latex] (already [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex] as-is) — void.
[latex][41],[35]\to[35,41][/latex] — not void.
[latex][25],[31]\to[25,31][/latex] (already in order) — void.

Next level (quads):
[latex][7,10]+[8,19]\to[7,8,10,19][/latex] (interleaved, not simply [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]) — not void.
[latex][35,41]+[25,31]\to[25,31,35,41][/latex] (interleaved) — not void.

Final merge:
[latex][7,8,10,19]+[25,31,35,41][/latex]: every element of the left ([latex]\le19[/latex]) is already smaller than every element of the right ([latex]\ge25[/latex]), so the merge is simply [latex]L[/latex] followed by [latex]R[/latex] — void.

Total merges [latex]=4+2+1=7[/latex] (matches the given count), with exactly [latex]3[/latex] of them void.

Answer: 3

text: Which of the following can be recurrence relation(s) corresponding to an algorithm with time complexity [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]?
solution:
Solve each recurrence and compare to [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]:

- [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+1[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=T(1)+(n-1)\times1=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches.
- [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+1[/latex]: by the Master theorem, [latex]a=2,b=2[/latex] so [latex]n^{\log_2 2}=n^1=n[/latex]; since [latex]f(n)=1[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n[/latex], Case 1 gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches.
- [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+n[/latex]: this is the classic merge-sort recurrence, [latex]f(n)=n=n^{\log_2 2}[/latex] exactly (Case 2), giving [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].
- [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+n[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(1+2+\cdots+n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].

Answer: T(n)=T(n-1)+1 and T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 both correspond to Θ(n) algorithms.

text:
Consider the following functions, where [latex]n[/latex] is a positive integer.

[latex] n^{1 / 3}, \log (n), \log (n!), 2^{\log (n)} [/latex]

Which one of the following options lists the functions in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate?
Note: Assume the base of log to be [latex]2[/latex].
solution:
Simplify each function's asymptotic growth (using [latex]\log[/latex] base [latex]2[/latex]):

- [latex]\log(n)[/latex]: grows the slowest of all — sub-polynomial.
- [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex]: a polynomial with a small (fractional) exponent, grows faster than any power of [latex]\log n[/latex] but slower than [latex]n[/latex] itself.
- [latex]2^{\log(n)}=n[/latex] (since exponentiating base [latex]2[/latex] by [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] simply recovers [latex]n[/latex]) — so this grows exactly like [latex]n[/latex], faster than [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex].
- [latex]\log(n!)[/latex]: by Stirling's approximation, [latex]\log(n!)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex], which grows faster than plain [latex]n[/latex] (and hence faster than [latex]2^{\log n}=n[/latex]).

So the increasing order is: [latex]\log(n) \;<\; n^{1/3} \;<\; 2^{\log(n)} \;<\; \log(n!)[/latex].

Answer: log(n), n^(1/3), 2^log(n), log(n!)

Consider the following pseudocode for depth-first search (DFS) algorithm which takes a directed graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] as input, where [latex]d[v][/latex] and [latex]f[v][/latex] are the discovery time and finishing time, respectively, of the vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex]. [latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \begin{array}{l} \textbf{DFS}(G): \\ \text{unmark all } v \in V \\ t \leftarrow 0 \\ \text{for each } v \in V \\ \quad \text{if } v \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,v,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \textbf{Explore}(G,v,t): \\ \text{mark } v \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ d[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{for each } (v,w) \in E \\ \quad \text{if } w \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,w,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ f[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{return } t \end{array} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Suppose that the input directed graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). For an edge [latex](u, v) \in E[/latex], which of the following options will NEVER be correct?
solution:
For a DAG, discovery/finish-time intervals [latex][d[v],f[v]][/latex] obtained from DFS obey the standard parenthesis theorem: for any two vertices, their intervals are either completely nested (one inside the other) or completely disjoint — they can never partially overlap.

For an edge [latex](u,v)[/latex] in a DAG, DFS classifies it as either a tree/forward edge (if [latex]v[/latex] is discovered while exploring from [latex]u[/latex], nesting [latex][d[v],f[v]][/latex] inside [latex][d[u],f[u]][/latex], giving [latex]d[u]cross edge (if [latex]v[/latex] was already fully explored before [latex]u[/latex] started, giving disjoint, non-overlapping intervals [latex]d[v]
- [latex]d[u] - [latex]d[v] - [latex]d[v]back edge — impossible in a DAG.
- [latex]d[u]never happen for any DFS on any graph, regardless of edge type.

Answer: [latex]d[v]

text: Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a simple, undirected, edge-weighted graph with unique edge weights. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees (MST) of [latex]G[/latex] is/are true?
solution:
When all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique, and two classical facts (cycle property and cut property) apply:

- Cycle property: In any cycle [latex]C[/latex], the edge with the strictly largest weight can never appear in any MST (if it did, removing it and adding any other edge of the cycle would still keep the graph connected but reduce total weight). True.
- The claim about the smallest-weight edge of every cycle being in every MST is false in general — a small edge can still be excluded if a smaller alternative path already connects its endpoints via other, even-cheaper edges from elsewhere in the graph (cycle property only rules out the *maximum*, it doesn't force in the minimum in the multi-cycle case with unrelated cycles overlapping).
- The claim that the largest-weight edge touching any given vertex [latex]v[/latex] is never in any MST is false — that edge might still be the cheapest way to connect an isolated/far-off part of the graph.
- Cut property: For any vertex [latex]v[/latex], consider the cut separating [latex]\{v\}[/latex] from the rest of the graph; the minimum-weight edge crossing this cut (i.e. the cheapest edge incident to [latex]v[/latex]) must belong to every MST, since choosing any costlier edge to connect [latex]v[/latex] instead would strictly increase total weight. True.

Answer: The largest-weight edge in every cycle is excluded from every MST; and the smallest-weight edge incident to every vertex is included in every MST.

Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be an undirected, edge-weighted graph with integer weights. The weight of a path is the sum of the weights of the edges in that path. The length of a path is the number of edges in that path.

Let [latex]s \in V[/latex] be a vertex in [latex]G[/latex]. For every [latex]u \in V[/latex] and for every [latex]k \geq 0[/latex], let [latex]d_{k}(u)[/latex] denote the weight of a shortest path (in terms of weight) from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]u[/latex] of length at most [latex]k[/latex]. If there is no path from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]u[/latex] of length at most [latex]k[/latex], then [latex]d_{k}(u)=\infty[/latex].

Consider the statements:

S1: For every [latex]k \geq 0[/latex] and [latex]u \in V, d_{k+1}(u) \leq d_{k}(u)[/latex].

S2: For every [latex](u, v) \in E[/latex], if [latex](u, v)[/latex] is part of a shortest path (in terms of weight) from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]v[/latex], then for every [latex]k \geq 0, d_{k}(u) \leq d_{k}(v)[/latex].

Which one of the following options is correct?
solution:
[latex]d_k(u)[/latex] is the shortest-path weight from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]u[/latex] using at most [latex]k[/latex] edges — this is exactly the quantity computed by the Bellman-Ford relaxation process after [latex]k[/latex] rounds.

S1: [latex]d_{k+1}(u)\le d_k(u)[/latex] — allowing one extra edge of "budget" can only give access to more paths (a path of length [latex]\le k[/latex] is also a path of length [latex]\le k+1[/latex]), so the shortest weight can only stay the same or decrease. True, always.

S2: Suppose [latex](u,v)[/latex] lies on a shortest path from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]v[/latex]; then [latex]d(v)=d(u)+w(u,v)\ge d(u)[/latex] in the limit, so eventually [latex]d_k(u)\le d_k(v)[/latex] once [latex]k[/latex] is large enough. But for small [latex]k[/latex] this need not hold: it's possible that [latex]u[/latex] has not yet been reached with a short enough path (so [latex]d_k(u)=\infty[/latex] is even bigger) or, more subtly, that a different, cheaper path of length [latex]\le k[/latex] to [latex]v[/latex] exists that doesn't go through [latex]u[/latex] at all — the inequality can fail for some particular [latex]k[/latex] even though it eventually holds in the limit. So S2 is not always true for every [latex]k[/latex].

Answer: Only S1 is true.

Consider the following recurrence relations:
For all [latex]n>1[/latex],

[latex] \begin{array}{l} T_{1}(n)=4 T_{1}\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+T_{2}(n) \\ T_{2}(n)=5 T_{2}\left(\frac{n}{4}\right)+\Theta\left(\log _{2} n\right) \end{array} [/latex]

Assume that for all [latex]n \leq 1, T_{1}(n)=1[/latex] and [latex]T_{2}(n)=1[/latex].
Which one of the following options is correct?
solution:
First solve [latex]T_2(n)=5T_2(n/4)+\Theta(\log_2 n)[/latex].
Here [latex]a=5,\,b=4[/latex], so [latex]n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_4 5}[/latex]. Since [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n^{\log_4 5}[/latex] (as [latex]\log_4 5\approx1.16>0[/latex]), by the Master theorem (Case 1):
[latex]T_2(n)=\Theta\left(n^{\log_4 5}\right)[/latex].

Now solve [latex]T_1(n)=4T_1(n/2)+T_2(n)[/latex].
Here [latex]a=4,\,b=2[/latex], so [latex]n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_2 4}=n^2[/latex]. The extra term [latex]f(n)=T_2(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_4 5})=\Theta(n^{1.16\ldots})[/latex], which is polynomially smaller than [latex]n^2[/latex] (since [latex]n^2/n^{1.16}=n^{0.84}\to\infty[/latex]).
By Master theorem Case 1: [latex]T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex]

Consider the following algorithm someAlgo that takes an undirected graph [latex]G[/latex] as input.

[latex]\texttt{someAlgo(G)}:[/latex]
1. Let [latex]v[/latex] be any vertex in [latex]G[/latex]. Run BFS on [latex]G[/latex] starting at [latex]v[/latex]. Let [latex]u[/latex] be a vertex in [latex]G[/latex] at maximum distance from [latex]v[/latex] as given by the BFS.
2. Run BFS on [latex]G[/latex] again with [latex]u[/latex] as the starting vertex. Let [latex]z[/latex] be the vertex at maximum distance from [latex]u[/latex] as given by the BFS.
3. Output the distance between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]z[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex].

The output of [latex]\texttt{someAlgo(T)}[/latex] for the tree shown in the given figure is __________. (Answer in integer)
solution:
This is the standard double-BFS algorithm for computing a tree's diameter (the longest path between any two nodes): BFS from an arbitrary vertex [latex]v[/latex] to find the farthest vertex [latex]u[/latex], then BFS again from [latex]u[/latex] to find the farthest vertex [latex]z[/latex] — the distance from [latex]u[/latex] to [latex]z[/latex] is guaranteed to equal the tree's true diameter (a classical, provable property specific to trees: whichever vertex is farthest from an arbitrary start must be one endpoint of some longest path).

Looking at the given tree: it has a central hub vertex from which several branches radiate outward — one branch (upper-left) extends out through a couple of intermediate vertices before forking further, another shorter branch goes off to the lower-left, and a branch on the right extends out and forks again near its far end. The two "longest reaching" branches from the hub are the upper-left branch and the right-hand branch.

Running BFS from any starting vertex [latex]v[/latex] will find some farthest vertex [latex]u[/latex] (this will land at the tip of one of the long branches, e.g. the far end of the upper-left branch). Running BFS again from [latex]u[/latex] then reaches all the way across the hub to the tip of the opposite long branch (the far end of the right-hand branch) as the new farthest vertex [latex]z[/latex]. Counting edges along this path — from the upper-left branch tip, back through its intermediate vertices, through the hub, and back out through the right-hand branch to its tip — gives a total of [latex]6[/latex] edges, matching the tree's actual diameter.

Answer: 6

text:
Let [latex]G [/latex] be an edge-weighted undirected graph with positive edge weights. Suppose a positive constant [latex]\alpha [/latex] is added to the weight of every edge.
Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE about the minimum spanning trees (MSTs) and shortest paths (SPs) in [latex]G [/latex] before and after the edge weight update?
solution:
Adding the same positive constant [latex]\alpha[/latex] to every edge shifts the total weight of any spanning tree by exactly [latex]\alpha\times(n-1)[/latex] (since every spanning tree has exactly [latex]n-1[/latex] edges, the same count) — a uniform shift that doesn't change which spanning tree has the minimum total weight. So every MST remains an MST.

Shortest paths, however, can use a different number of edges depending on the route — a path with fewer edges gets a smaller total addition of [latex]\alpha[/latex] than a path with more edges, which can flip which path is actually shortest after the update. So SPs need not remain SPs.

Answer: Every MST remains an MST, and SPs need not remain SPs.

text: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph [latex]G [/latex] is/are TRUE?
solution:
Checking each BFS/DFS claim on an undirected simple graph:

- "A DFS tree is a shortest path tree": false — DFS explores as deep as possible along one branch first and gives no shortest-path guarantee at all; only BFS guarantees that.
- "Every non-tree edge w.r.t. a DFS tree is a forward/back edge": true — in an undirected graph, DFS can never produce a cross edge; every non-tree edge necessarily connects an ancestor-descendant pair (classified as a back edge, viewable from either endpoint as forward/back).
- "Non-tree BFS edge (u,v): distances differ by at most 1": true — this is a standard BFS property, since BFS explores level-by-level and any edge can only connect vertices in the same level or adjacent levels.
- "Both BFS and DFS can find connected components": true — running either traversal repeatedly from every yet-unvisited vertex correctly partitions the graph into its connected components.

Answer: The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th statements are all true.

text: Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be an undirected and unweighted graph with 100 vertices. Let [latex]d(u, v)[/latex] denote the number of edges in a shortest path between vertices [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] in [latex]V[/latex]. Let the maximum value of [latex]d(u, v)[/latex], [latex]u, v \in V[/latex] such that [latex]u \neq v[/latex], be 30. Let [latex]T[/latex] be any breadth-first-search tree of [latex]G[/latex]. Which ONE of the given options is CORRECT for every such graph [latex]G[/latex]?
solution:
Let the diameter of the graph be the maximum shortest distance between any two vertices.
It is given that [latex] \max_{u,v\in V,\;u\ne v} d(u,v)=30. [/latex]
Thus, the diameter of the graph is 30.

Relation between BFS Tree Height and Graph Diameter

A Breadth-First Search (BFS) tree rooted at a vertex (r) has the following property:

- The level of every vertex equals its shortest distance from the root.
- Therefore, the height of the BFS tree is the maximum shortest distance from the root to any vertex, which is called the eccentricity of the root.

Let the height of the BFS tree be (h). Then, [latex] h=\max_{v\in V} d(r,v). [/latex]

Using the Diameter

Let the diameter of the graph be (D=30). A well-known property of graphs is [latex] \text{Radius} \ge \left\lceil\frac{D}{2}\right\rceil. [/latex]

Since [latex] D=30, [/latex] we get [latex] \left\lceil\frac{30}{2}\right\rceil=15. [/latex]

Every vertex has eccentricity at least the radius. Hence, regardless of the chosen BFS root, [latex] h\ge 15. [/latex]

The height need not be exactly 15 or exactly 30. It can be any value between 15 and 30 depending on the chosen root.

For example:

- If the BFS starts from a central vertex, the height can be 15.
- If it starts from an end vertex of a diameter, the height can be 30.

Correct Answer: (C) The height of (T) is at least 15.

text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be any undirected graph with positive edge weights, and [latex]T[/latex] be a minimum spanning tree of [latex]G[/latex]. [latex]T[/latex] is a subgraph of [latex]G[/latex] using only a subset of [latex]G[/latex]'s edges, so any path that exists inside [latex]T[/latex] between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] is also a valid path in [latex]G[/latex] (with the exact same total weight). text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be an undirected connected graph in which every edge has a positive integer weight.  Suppose  that  every  spanning  tree  in  [latex]G[/latex]  has  even  weight.  Which  of  the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph [latex]G[/latex] ?
solution:
Take any cycle C and two edges [latex]e,f[/latex] on it. Extend the path [latex]C-f[/latex] to a spanning tree T (it contains [latex]e[/latex], not [latex]f[/latex]). Then [latex]T'=T-e+f[/latex] is also a spanning tree.

[latex]w(T')-w(T)=w(f)-w(e)[/latex]. Both trees are even, so [latex]w(f)-w(e)[/latex] is even [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]e[/latex] and [latex]f[/latex] have the same parity. So in every cycle all edges are even or all are odd [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Counter-examples for the rest:
- Triangle with all weights 1: every spanning tree has weight 2 (even), yet edges are odd [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] options 1 and 3 FALSE.
- Path with weights 1, 1, 2: only spanning tree has weight 4, but edges are mixed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] option 2 FALSE.

Answer: In each cycle, either all edges have even weight OR all edges have odd weight
